chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Ibn Sinan, from Abdullah ibn Muskan and Salih al-Nayli, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, hates an abundance of sleep and an abundance of idleness.

key_terms.النَّوْم: Sleep — natural necessity but condemned when excessive
key_terms.الْفَرَاغ: Emptiness, idleness, leisure — time spent without productive work or worship
key_terms.كَثْرَة: Excess, abundance, overabundance — here indicating a blameworthy degree beyond need

ai.seo_question: What does Islam say about excessive sleep and idleness?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) conveys a divine displeasure with two interconnected vices: excessive sleep and excessive idleness. This teaching was directed at the early Muslim community in Kufa, where spiritual and economic productivity were closely linked. The Imam's audience would have understood this as a call to vigilance — both in fulfilling religious duties that require wakefulness and in contributing to the community through work and trade, topics discussed in the broader chapter on the dislike of sleep and leisure.

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Khalid, from his father, from Ibn Sinan, from Abdullah Bin Muskan, and Salih Al Nayli, from Abu Baseer, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Mighty and Majestic Hates the abundance of the sleep and the abundance of the leisure time’.
en.sarwar: 3. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from his father from ibn Sinan from ‘Abd Allah ibn Muskan from Salih al-Niliy who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘
Allah, most Majestic, most Glorious, hates one’s excessive sleeping and passing time without work.’”
